title: The Battery and the Heat: Derating Before Stopping, Voltage That Sags Under Load, and a Resume Point Above the Stop Point

questions.question: Why derate before stopping?
options: Derating uses less of the battery than stopping does
A robot told to slow down has time to reach somewhere safe, and a robot cut off where it stands may not
A stop is not allowed by the standard without a warning
Derating cools the motor faster than stopping
questions.explanation: At half power the robot can still drive to a safe place. Cut off outright it stays where it is, which may be the worst place.

questions.question: A battery at 22.0 V at rest drives 15 A through 0.1 ohm. What do the terminals read, and what should a monitor judge it as?
options: 20.5 at the terminals, and it should be judged at 20.5: that is what the motors get
22.0 at the terminals: a healthy battery does not sag
20.5 at the terminals, and 22.0 once the sag is added back: the battery has lost nothing
23.5 at the terminals, since current raises the voltage
questions.explanation: 15 A through 0.1 ohm drops 1.5 V inside the battery. Adding it back gives the resting voltage, which is what says how much charge is left.

questions.question: A battery sits at its stop voltage with a little noise. What happens with a resume point equal to the stop voltage?
options: It stops once and stays stopped
It runs at half power
Nothing: noise is below the threshold
It stops and starts again over and over
questions.explanation: 135 stops in 600 samples against 1 with a resume at 21.0 V. At the threshold noise carries the reading across it again and again. A resume point above the stop point means it has to recover properly before it restarts.

questions.question: Why did the hard stop run for an hour with 53 stops and almost the same mean power as derating?
options: Heat was only dealt with at the limit
The hard stop cools the motor better each time it stops
Its limit was set 20 degrees higher than the derating one
It did far more work, at the cost of a few stops
questions.explanation: It hit the limit again each time: the work done was about the same, with a hotter machine that kept stopping. Running flat out until the limit and then stopping gave almost the same work, 0.85 against 0.81, with a peak at the limit 53 times. Derating settled where heating and cooling balance.

questions.question: A thermistor wire comes off and reads 200 degrees. What should the monitor do?
options: Derate to half power until it reads sensibly
Ignore it and use the last good reading
Stop: a reading outside the plausible range cannot be real and not knowing is a stop
Treat it as 80 degrees, the stop limit
questions.explanation: 200 degrees is not a temperature the motor can have. The monitor does not know the real one, and not knowing is a stop; a good reading brings it back.

questions.question: What does this monitor not do that a lithium pack needs?
options: Measure the current drawn
Allow for the sag under load
Stop on a reading that cannot be real
Watch the cells one by one, which is where fires start, and it cannot stand in for the battery's own protection
questions.explanation: The monitor sees the pack as one voltage. A lithium pack fails cell by cell, and that needs the battery's own protection circuit.
